section_summary: This section documents growing U.S. concern over Japanese-linked narcotics trafficking, especially morphine and cocaine carried by ship to Hawaii and the Pacific Coast, and the diplomatic arrangements for routing investigations through the American Embassy and Japanese Foreign Office. It contains reports on several smuggling rings, arrests, prosecutions, seizures, and disputed Japanese sentences, together with newspaper clippings and cross-references concerning Japan, China, Manchuria, and the United States. The section also covers League of Nations drug-control reporting and Japanese studies of kava use in the South Seas Mandate.

subfiles.title: Treasury concurrence in routing Japanese narcotics investigations through the Embassy
subfiles.from: H. W. Roberts, Assistant Secretary of the Treasury
subfiles.about: The Treasury accepts the State Department's proposal that requests for Japanese narcotics investigations be presented through the American Embassy at Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: The letter acknowledges the State Department's confidential communication of April 18 concerning drugs of Japanese manufacture smuggled into the United States. Although the Treasury attaché at Kobe had investigative capacity, Treasury agrees temporarily to route requests through the Embassy and Japanese Foreign Office.

subfiles.title: Instruction to present narcotics cases through the Japanese Foreign Office
subfiles.about: The Embassy is instructed to submit narcotics cases to the Japanese Foreign Office pending further instructions.
subfiles.summary: State reports that the Treasury Department has agreed to instruct its personnel in Japan to work through the Embassy. The confidential cable directs the Embassy to present relevant cases to the Japanese Foreign Office for investigation.

subfiles.title: Confidential file divider, 894.114 Narcotics/79
subfiles.about: A confidential file sheet separates records in the narcotics case.
subfiles.summary: The page contains only the file number and a confidential-file notation. It serves as an internal divider rather than substantive correspondence.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Tientsin despatch on the local heroin trade
subfiles.about: The sheet cross-references a despatch reporting that Japanese manufacturers and distributors dominated Tientsin's rapidly growing heroin trade.
subfiles.summary: The referenced despatch states that Japanese traffickers had emphasized heroin production during the preceding four years. Japanese experts allegedly established themselves in North China and produced heroin at prices well below those in Europe.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to telegram on the arrest of Tatsujiro Kawahara
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a telegram reporting Kawahara's arrest and Sugimoto's implication in the same case.
subfiles.summary: The filing note records the arrest of Tatsujiro Kawahara in Japan. It adds that Sugimoto of the Chichibu Maru was also implicated.

subfiles.title: Treasury request for duplicate distribution of narcotics-smuggling correspondence
subfiles.about: Treasury asks State to send duplicate copies of narcotics correspondence to both the Customs and Narcotics commissioners.
subfiles.summary: Treasury states that the Bureau of Customs had not known about the direct information-exchange arrangement with Japanese narcotics authorities. Because Customs and the Narcotic Service share responsibility for suppressing smuggling, it requests duplicate copies of all formal or confidential communications.

subfiles.title: State Department explanation of the U.S.–Japan narcotics information agreement
subfiles.about: State explains the origins of the direct information exchange with Japan and proposes a conference to improve liaison.
subfiles.summary: The letter says the exchange arrangement arose from a 1927 Treasury suggestion and that Treasury was notified in 1928 and again in 1929. It invokes the 1931 Narcotics Limitation Convention and proposes a meeting between Treasury officials and Stuart J. Fuller of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding correspondence on Japanese-origin narcotics seizures
subfiles.about: State forwards correspondence concerning narcotics seizures and clarifies when direct replies by the Commissioner of Narcotics are acceptable.
subfiles.summary: The instruction recalls earlier telegrams about sending seizure inquiries through the Embassy. It encloses communications between U.S. and Japanese narcotics officials and permits a direct reply in one instance because the Japanese inquiry concerned only a minor detail.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese statement on narcotics manufacturers and dealers
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a despatch containing a Japanese representative's statement about narcotics manufacturers and dealers.
subfiles.summary: This filing note points to despatch No. 354 in another decimal-file location. Its subject is a statement by a Japanese representative concerning manufacturers and dealers in narcotic drugs.

subfiles.title: Request for press coverage of illicit Japanese narcotics traffic
subfiles.about: The Embassy is asked to collect press reports on narcotics traffic between Japan and other countries, especially the U.S. Pacific Coast.
subfiles.summary: State requests English-language clippings and translations from Japanese publications. It identifies the Japan Chronicle of Kobe as a likely source and emphasizes the serious scale of trafficking to the Pacific Coast.

subfiles.title: Transmission of the Netherlands Indies annual drug report
subfiles.about: State transmits copies of the Netherlands Indies annual report on opium and dangerous drugs.
subfiles.summary: The report was submitted under the 1931 Narcotics Limitation Convention and forwarded by the League of Nations. Extra copies are provided for the Commissioner of Narcotics and the Customs Agency Service.

subfiles.title: Request for details of the Osaka narcotics-smuggling judgments
subfiles.about: The consul is asked to investigate reports of enormous fines imposed on a gang that smuggled drugs from Germany into Japan.
subfiles.summary: Available reports lacked the defendants' names, the drugs and sources involved, the destination of the contraband, and details of imprisonment or appeal. State asks the consul to obtain a full account from the appropriate authorities.

subfiles.title: Standing request for narcotics newspaper clippings from Kobe
subfiles.about: The Kobe Consulate is instructed to send available narcotics-related newspaper clippings in each diplomatic pouch.
subfiles.summary: The Department seeks English-language clippings and translations concerning illicit opium or drug traffic in Japan. It is particularly concerned about the growing traffic between Japan and the U.S. Pacific Coast.

subfiles.title: Despatch transmitting Japanese information on arrested narcotics traffickers
subfiles.about: Grew forwards a translated Foreign Ministry note concerning recently arrested traffickers.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure includes a Japanese Foreign Ministry communication and an annex previously sent to Commissioner Anslinger. Grew highlights that the traffickers received penalties of only one month's imprisonment.

subfiles.title: Hirota note transmitting Kuriyama's narcotics communication
subfiles.from: Koki Hirota, Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.about: Hirota sends Grew copies of Kuriyama's communication to U.S. Narcotics Commissioner Anslinger.
subfiles.summary: The note formally transmits information on narcotics traffickers recently arrested by Japanese authorities. It identifies S. Kuriyama and H. J. Anslinger as the officials directly corresponding on the case.

subfiles.title: Kuriyama report and annex on three maritime narcotics-smuggling groups
subfiles.from: S. Kuriyama, Director of the Bureau of Treaties and Conventions
subfiles.to: H. J. Anslinger, Commissioner, Bureau of Narcotics
subfiles.about: Kuriyama supplies detailed Japanese police information on three groups smuggling cocaine or morphine between Japan and the United States.
subfiles.summary: The annex describes the Takenaga group carrying cocaine aboard the Asama Maru to San Francisco, the Nakamura group moving morphine obtained in Hong Kong, and the Nishijima–Matsuzaki shipment aboard the Tatsuta Maru to Los Angeles. It gives names, occupations, addresses, dates, methods of discovery, suppliers, and alleged American recipients. Manufacturers were generally unknown, and Nishijima and Matsuzaki received one-month penal-servitude sentences.

subfiles.title: Instruction on the expanding flow of Japanese narcotics to the Pacific Coast
subfiles.about: State sends seizure evidence for discreet use in pressing Japanese authorities to suppress narcotics trafficking.
subfiles.summary: The instruction says seizures involving Japanese persons, ships, or drugs increased sharply in early 1933 and helped reduce illicit morphine prices on the Pacific Coast. It contrasts five-year U.S. sentences imposed on Nishiyori, Takata, and Mayeda with the very short Japanese sentences imposed on Fujihara, Kondo, Kawahara, and Sugimoto.

subfiles.title: List of U.S. narcotics seizures involving Japan, 1932–1933
subfiles.about: The list catalogs American seizures involving Japanese nationals, vessels, or drugs of Japanese origin from January 1932 through June 1933.
subfiles.summary: Cases occurred in Honolulu, Seattle, Tacoma, Los Angeles, Scappoose, and New York and involved cocaine medicines, smoking opium, morphine, and poppy heads. The entries identify labels, vessels, quantities, and persons arrested, illustrating the maritime character and widening scale of the trade.

subfiles.title: Despatch transmitting a clipping on cocaine smuggling at Osaka
subfiles.about: Donovan forwards an Osaka Mainichi article and describes the Consulate's plan for regular narcotics-clipping submissions.
subfiles.summary: The enclosed article concerns a group of cocaine smugglers arrested by the Kobe Water Police. Donovan states that future pouches will carry relevant clippings from the Kobe consular district, including U.S. prosecutions unless instructed otherwise.

subfiles.title: “Smugglers of Cocaine Arrested by the Kobe Water Police Station”
subfiles.about: The article reports the arrest of a group accused of repeatedly smuggling cocaine to San Francisco.
subfiles.summary: It names Sumizo Matsunaga, Denzo Yanagida, Seiichi Morita, and Tokuji Ai and alleges that the sailors were used to move cocaine aboard the Asama Maru. The paper claims the ring made five shipments worth ¥15,000 in total.

subfiles.title: Detailed report on the Osaka German-morphine smuggling case
subfiles.about: Donovan summarizes the court record of six men convicted of importing large quantities of morphine compounds from Hamburg.
subfiles.summary: The despatch identifies the defendants, German suppliers, quantities, distribution network, appeals, prison terms, fines, and compulsory compensation for drugs already sold. Donovan argues that the nominal fines convertible into short periods of prison labor were largely farcical, while additional confiscatory assessments represented substantial, enforceable liabilities. Four defendants appealed to the Supreme Court in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Osaka Asahi report on record fines and forfeitures
subfiles.about: The clipping reports fines and forfeitures totaling about ¥6.7 million against six narcotics traffickers.
subfiles.summary: The article lists the six defendants and the penalties imposed by Judge Onishi's court. It characterizes the aggregate financial punishment as unprecedented.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to poppy cultivation in Manchukuo
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a despatch enclosing a Japan Times clipping on poppy cultivation in Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: This is an internal reference to despatch No. 570. Its stated subject is the cultivation of the poppy in Manchukuo.

subfiles.title: Transmission of the Kobe report on the Osaka smuggling case
subfiles.about: State forwards the Kobe Consulate's despatch on the Osaka narcotics-smuggling case to the Commissioner of Narcotics.
subfiles.summary: The note encloses despatch No. 240 and its supporting material. It is intended for the Bureau of Narcotics' information and records.

subfiles.title: Status report on Supreme Court appeal by Osaka narcotics smugglers
subfiles.about: The Consulate General reports that the smugglers' Supreme Court appeal will be heard in the near future.
subfiles.summary: The despatch follows the Kobe Consulate's report on convictions arising from narcotics operations around Osaka. Information obtained through the Embassy and Foreign Ministry gives no firm hearing date, but the Consulate promises a later report.

subfiles.title: Confidential transmission of the Supreme Court appeal status
subfiles.about: State confidentially forwards the Tokyo Consulate General's update on the Osaka smugglers' appeal.
subfiles.summary: The note supplements State's November 22 communication to Treasury. It encloses despatch No. 724 for the Commissioner of Narcotics.

subfiles.title: Detached continuation of report on Shakao or kava
subfiles.about: This detached page continues a discussion of kava's medicinal effects, possible toxicity, and regulated use on Pohnpei.
subfiles.summary: The excerpt says the active ingredient is excreted in urine and that kava was used medicinally for local paralysis, gonorrhea, and catarrhal complaints. It describes “kawaismus,” denies that kava is alcoholic or morphine-like, and says Japanese authorities limited use to once weekly; no toxicity cases had been reported under the mandate.

subfiles.title: Transmission of clipping on the Taiyo Maru narcotics arrests
subfiles.about: State sends Treasury a Japan Advertiser clipping about two Chinese crewmen accused of attempting to smuggle narcotics into the United States.
subfiles.summary: The clipping concerns cocaine and morphine valued at ¥27,000 aboard the Taiyo Maru. It is forwarded specifically for the information of the Commissioner of Narcotics.

subfiles.title: “Narcotics Found on Ship”
subfiles.about: The article reports the arrest of two Chinese crewmen after narcotics were discovered aboard the Taiyo Maru.
subfiles.summary: Cocaine and morphine were hidden under tables and in fire-bucket lockers, then thrown overboard on the captain's orders before docking at Yokohama. Police arrested cabin boy Chao Tze-tung and interpreter Lien Tai and suspected that they were agents of a larger ring.

subfiles.title: Transmission of the Japanese report excerpt on Pohnpei kava
subfiles.about: State transmits an excerpt on native kava use from Japan's 1932 report on the South Seas Mandate.
subfiles.summary: The note observes that kava use in the South Seas was long known. It emphasizes Japanese study of the plant's narcotic properties and efforts to isolate its active principle.

subfiles.title: Japanese annual-report excerpt on Shakao or Sakao
subfiles.about: The excerpt describes the preparation, ceremonial use, botany, cultivation, and physiological effects of kava on Pohnpei.
subfiles.summary: Pohnpei inhabitants prepared Shakao from pounded roots for communal ceremonies and consumed it according to social rank. The report identifies the plant as Piper methysticum, describes its cultivation and sedative effects, and discusses competing explanations for its active ingredients.

subfiles.title: Transmission of kava excerpt for the Surgeon General
subfiles.about: State sends the Pohnpei kava excerpt for the information of the Surgeon General of the U.S. Public Health Service.
subfiles.summary: The note repeats that Japanese authorities were studying kava's narcotic properties and attempting to extract its active principle. The document is routed through Treasury for public-health review.

subfiles.title: Treasury acknowledgment of the kava report excerpt
subfiles.from: H. W. Roberts, Assistant Secretary of the Treasury
subfiles.about: Treasury acknowledges receipt of the Japanese annual-report excerpt concerning kava use on Pohnpei.
subfiles.summary: The letter identifies State's December 19 communication and the source report on the South Seas Mandate for 1932. It confirms receipt for the Surgeon General's information.

subfiles.title: File jacket: Traffic in Narcotics—Japan, case 150
subfiles.about: The page is a case-file jacket for records concerning narcotics traffic in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The jacket bears subject and case-number information and a December 1933 date stamp. It instructs users not to disarrange, remove, stamp, or annotate the papers.

subfiles.title: Report that the Supreme Court upheld the Osaka convictions
subfiles.about: Donovan reports that Japan's Supreme Court rejected the appeal of Keiji Kitada and his five codefendants.
subfiles.summary: On December 9 the Supreme Court confirmed the Osaka Court of Appeals judgment in the German-morphine case. Donovan encloses a Japan Advertiser clipping announcing the decision.

subfiles.title: “Fine on Smugglers Is Upheld by Court”
subfiles.about: The article reports that the Supreme Court upheld penalties totaling more than ¥6.8 million against six drug smugglers.
subfiles.summary: The defendants allegedly imported 3,784 kilograms of morphine compounds from Germany in 67 consignments between 1928 and 1931. The article lists each man's prison term, fine, and compensation owed to the state.

subfiles.title: “New Example of Judgment on Smuggling of Morphine”
subfiles.about: The article explains the Supreme Court's valuation rule for confiscatory assessments in morphine-smuggling cases.
subfiles.summary: The court rejected the defense argument that valuation should be based on prices at judgment or on the absence of a lawful market. It held that compensation must reflect the market price when the crime occurred, less import duty, establishing a precedent for later cases.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Japan Advertiser report on the upheld smuggling fines
subfiles.about: This duplicate article reports the rejection of the six defendants' Supreme Court appeal.
subfiles.summary: It repeats that the ring imported thousands of kilograms of morphine compounds from Germany in 67 consignments. Individual fines, imprisonment, and state compensation orders are itemized.

subfiles.title: “Notorious Drug Smugglers Told by Court to Pay Up ¥6,802,367”
subfiles.about: The Japan Times reports the Supreme Court's confirmation of heavy fines and compensation orders against six narcotics smugglers.
subfiles.summary: The article says the defendants imported about 3,794 kilograms of morphine compounds from Germany between 1928 and 1931. It lists the sentences and financial liabilities of Kitada, Asada, Shimamura, Inohara, Miyamoto, and Yajima.

subfiles.title: “Morphine from Japan Problem to America”
subfiles.about: The article summarizes Anslinger's warning that Japanese morphine had become a major source of illicit supply on the U.S. Pacific Coast and in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: Anslinger's annual report states that the heaviest morphine seizures occurred on the Pacific Coast and that the contraband came almost entirely by ship from Japan. It describes Japanese smuggling and distribution as a new development causing grave concern to American and Canadian authorities.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Japan's 1932 League of Nations drug report
subfiles.about: State forwards Japan's 1932 report on opium and dangerous drugs for the Surgeon General's information.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure is League of Nations document O.C./A.R. 1932/39, dated November 20, 1933. It reports on Japan's traffic in opium and other dangerous drugs during 1932.

subfiles.title: Embassy copy of Japan's 1932 drug-traffic report
subfiles.about: State sends the Embassy a copy of Japan's League of Nations report for 1932 on opium and dangerous drugs.
subfiles.summary: The instruction identifies the document by its League of Nations number. It is furnished for the Embassy's information without further action specified.

subfiles.title: Treasury acknowledgment of Japan's 1932 drug report
subfiles.from: H. W. Roberts, Assistant Secretary of the Treasury
subfiles.about: Treasury acknowledges receipt of Japan's 1932 report on opium and other dangerous drugs.
subfiles.summary: The letter cites State's December 28 communication and League document O.C./A.R. 1932/39. Receipt is confirmed for the Surgeon General of the Public Health Service.

subfiles.title: Transmission of the final decision in the Osaka smuggling case
subfiles.about: State sends the Commissioner of Narcotics Donovan's report that the Supreme Court upheld the Osaka sentences.
subfiles.summary: The note follows earlier correspondence about the German-morphine smuggling gang. It encloses consular despatch No. 262 and the December 10 Japan Advertiser clipping.

subfiles.title: “Morphine Runner Seized”
subfiles.about: The article describes a reactionary activist whose smuggled-morphine transaction inadvertently benefited Communist fundraising.
subfiles.summary: Toyoji Harada was arrested after accusing a chemist of substituting sugar and flour for morphine he had left at the shop. Police learned that he had sold four pounds to Teruo Ishii and Akihiko Tsurumaru, who allegedly planned to resell it to finance Communist activities.

subfiles.title: “League's Narcotics Board Not Worried by Big Needs”
subfiles.about: The clipping reports 1934 global drug estimates and concern over Japan's unusually large heroin requirement.
subfiles.summary: The League supervisory board estimated worldwide requirements of 47 tons of morphine, cocaine, and heroin, including 40 tons of morphine. Japan, including Korea and Formosa, was allotted 650 kilograms of heroin and reportedly requested more than half as much as the rest of the world combined.

subfiles.title: “47 Tons of Morphine, Cocaine and Heroin to Be Used in 1934”
subfiles.about: The clipping gives the League's 1934 narcotics estimates and repeats concern over Japan's heroin allocation.
subfiles.summary: It reports aggregate requirements for 68 countries and 114 territories and colonies. Japan, Korea, and Formosa account for an exceptionally large share of requested heroin, while import and export certificates are to verify national quotas.

subfiles.title: “Opium Smugglers Arrested”
subfiles.about: The article reports the arrest of four people seeking buyers for opium obtained from a Japanese railway employee in Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: Takatsu police in Kanagawa Prefecture made the arrests. The seized opium was valued at ¥2,500.

subfiles.title: “The Reorientation of ‘Dope’”
subfiles.about: The editorial assesses the shift in international narcotics supply toward Japan and China after European production controls.
subfiles.summary: It acknowledges reduced legal morphine and cocaine production but warns that Japanese morphine was appearing in Hawaii, the Pacific Coast, China, and Manchuria. The editorial considers Japanese participation potentially controllable through publicity and pressure, while depicting China's officially protected opium production and internal traffic as a larger and less tractable danger. It cites large escorted opium movements in Guizhou and Guangxi and the fiscal dependence of Chinese military and provincial authorities on the trade.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on narcotics found aboard the President Madison
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a despatch stating that the origin of narcotics found aboard the President Madison could not be determined.
subfiles.summary: The referenced seizure occurred in Seattle on August 9, 1932. Grew's despatch reported that investigators were unable to establish where the drugs originated.

subfiles.title: Transmission of two Japan Advertiser narcotics articles
subfiles.about: State sends Treasury copies of “Morphine Runner Seized” and “Narcotic Sale Stopped.”
subfiles.summary: The articles appeared in the Japan Advertiser on December 17 and 19, 1933. Copies are supplied to both the Commissioner of Narcotics and the Commissioner of Customs.

subfiles.title: Second copy of “Morphine Runner Seized”
subfiles.about: This copy recounts the Harada morphine affair and its connection to Communist fundraising.
subfiles.summary: Toyoji Harada attempted to sell morphine allegedly smuggled through Sakhalin and later accused a chemist of substituting harmless material. Investigation linked his earlier sale to Teruo Ishii and Akihiko Tsurumaru, who intended to raise money for Communist organizations.

subfiles.title: “Narcotic Sale Stopped”
subfiles.about: The damaged clipping reports arrests made while narcotics were changing hands in an illicit Tokyo transaction.
subfiles.summary: The legible text links the drug to an employee of the South Manchuria Railway Company and names Ukichi Hirayama and several other alleged participants. Police learned of the planned sale and raided the meeting as the transaction was taking place.

subfiles.title: Report on the arrest of opium dealers at Osaka
subfiles.about: Donovan reports the arrest of a Chinese opium peddler and the comparatively light treatment of his Japanese supplier.
subfiles.summary: Ling Cheng Sui, also identified by Japanese readings and an alias, was caught with 296 grams of opium after an alleged ten-year trade among Osaka's Chinese residents. He was held for trial, whereas supplier Manjiro Nakao received a final fine of only ¥250. Donovan notes the apparent disparity in their treatment.

subfiles.title: Confidential transmission of the Osaka opium-arrest report
subfiles.about: State confidentially forwards Donovan's despatch about two opium smugglers arrested at Osaka.
subfiles.summary: The note encloses despatch No. 273 of January 13, 1934, from Kobe. It is intended for the confidential information of the Commissioner of Narcotics.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding “The Reorientation of ‘Dope’”
subfiles.about: State sends the Embassy the New York Herald-Tribune editorial on Far Eastern opium and narcotics traffic.
subfiles.summary: The instruction encloses the March 5 article for the Embassy's information. The editorial addresses both Japanese and Chinese roles in the regional drug trade.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on sharing narcotics information with the Japanese consul at Seattle
subfiles.about: Treasury requests State's views on authorizing communication of narcotics information to the Japanese consul at Seattle.
subfiles.summary: The filing note points to another file containing Treasury's request. Its subject is the advisability of sharing investigative information with the Japanese consular representative.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Saigon report on Japanese promotion of addiction
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a report alleging Japanese efforts to increase drug addiction and sales in North China and Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The referenced report claims that Japan was actively promoting addiction in the two regions. It further alleges the sale of large quantities of drugs there.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Shanghai report on narcotics manufacturing
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a Shanghai police report concerning Japanese and Cantonese involvement in narcotics manufacture.
subfiles.summary: The underlying report concerns the recent opium situation in the Shanghai International Settlement. It notes Japanese and Cantonese participation in narcotics manufacturing and names G. Nagasawa as an accused person.

subfiles.title: “Guilty of Dope Traffic”
subfiles.from: Osaka Mainichi and Tokyo Nichi Nichi
subfiles.about: The clipping reports Sennosuke Asai's prosecution for violating narcotics and tariff regulations.
subfiles.summary: Asai, also known as Shinso Otake and described as a co-partner of the Dance Palace in Amagasaki, was found guilty during examination at the Osaka District Procurators' Office. He was detained at the Kita branch prison and arraigned.
